content: Potassium iodate (KIO3) is a chemical compound with several applications in medicine and industry. It is sometimes utilized in radiation treatment due to its ability to displace radioactive iodine from the thyroid gland. For further details on this application, refer to potassium iodide, which is closely related in function. In the food industry, potassium iodate is occasionally employed as a maturing agent in baking, similar to potassium bromate. Chemically, potassium iodate is classified as an oxidizing agent. This property makes it potentially hazardous, as it can ignite fires when it comes into contact with combustible materials or reducing agents. Potassium iodate can be synthesized through a reaction between a potassium-containing base, such as potassium hydroxide (KOH), and iodic acid (HIO3). The reaction proceeds as follows: HIO3 + KOH → KIO3 + H2O Alternatively, it can be produced by adding iodine (I2) to a hot, concentrated solution of potassium hydroxide. One of the primary uses of potassium iodate is in the iodination of table salt. This is because potassium iodide, another iodine source, can be oxidized to iodine under moist conditions in the presence of oxygen. To prevent this oxidation, manufacturers in the United States typically add thiosulfates or other antioxidants to potassium iodide. However, in some other countries, potassium iodate is directly used as the iodine source in table salt.
